name: Aaron Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Northfield Farms, which is big: 900 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, plus three chicken sheds with about 40,000 birds each. I start at six walking the sheds, checking water lines and picking out any dead birds, which nobody tells you about when you sign up. Then I'm usually on the sprayer or in the grain store. I'm a year and a half in, the most junior man on the place at 58.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-eight years selling cars at a dealership on the ring road. I was good at it, but I got sick of the suit and the targets, and my wife Selin said, you're always talking about the countryside, so go. I'm still learning everything, I'm slow on the sprayer settings. But I use the AI on my phone constantly, I ask it about fungus on the barley, I get it to explain the soil reports, I even practise the agronomy words with it on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, shame, I was looking forward to it. I'd say it at lunch in the grain store and the lads would laugh at me. I'd still tell anyone who'd listen that the tools we've got now are worth learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much changes for me, and I'd be a bit disappointed. I've been using these tools every day, they've made me a better farmhand faster than I'd have managed on my own. I'd have liked to see what came next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, keep using the AI to learn the job faster, and keep pushing Phil, the farm manager, to try the crop-scouting drone the dealer showed us. Money-wise, nothing changes, we've got the house paid off and a decent pile from my sales years. I'd still try to get my spraying certificate this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, which I know sounds odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed, when it keeps your job safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's like a test drive. You don't know if the car's any good till you've had it on the motorway. I'd rather know what this thing can do than read about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd do this year regardless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do the spraying certificate, which would get me a bit more pay and more interesting work. And I'd keep nagging Phil about the drone, because walking 900 hectares of barley looking for fungus is a lot of walking.

S0.say: I'd say shame, I was looking forward to it, and the lads would laugh at me at lunch. I'd still tell anyone the tools we've got now are worth learning.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me, and I'd be a bit disappointed. These tools have made me a better farmhand faster than I'd have managed alone.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to learn the job, pushes the farm manager to try a crop-scouting drone and gets his spraying certificate this winter. Leaves money plans alone, with a paid-off house and savings from his sales years.
S0.quote: It's like a test drive. You don't know if the car's any good till you've had it on the motorway.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is a former car salesman who treats new technology like a test drive. He is secure financially and eager to learn, so the quiet picture slightly disappoints him. He uses AI daily to make up for coming to farming late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, it's like when cars went from carburettors to computers, the mechanics who learned the new stuff did fine. I'd say it at the grain store and online. Some people would lose out, sure, and the government should help them, but most of us can move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do well. I'm the one already using it, and I'm not precious about how things used to be done, because I don't know how they used to be done. Being new is actually a help here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the drone man at Northfield, take the training the dealer offers and take the farm's scouting off Phil's hands. I'd do the spraying certificate and maybe a short course on running autonomous machines, there's one at the agricultural college. And I'd move some of our savings into a fund of farm technology companies, a modest amount, maybe ten thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite keen. Like the first week at a new dealership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who's done the chicken sheds for fifteen years and hates his phone. And the two seasonal lads from abroad who do the summer harvest. If the combines drive themselves, those seasonal jobs go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him, honestly. It worked for me. I'd sit with him on lunch break and show him how to ask the phone about a sick bird, like I'd show a customer the sat nav.

S1.say: I'd say it's like cars going from carburettors to computers: the mechanics who learned the new stuff did fine. Some people would lose out and government should help them, but most of us can move with it.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I already use it and I'm not precious about the old ways. Being new to farming actually helps here.
S1.do: Volunteers to run the farm's drone scouting and takes the dealer's training, plus his spraying certificate and a college course on autonomous machines. Puts about 10,000 of savings into a farm technology fund, and coaches a colleague on the phone tools.
S1.feel: Calm and quite keen, like the first week at a new dealership.
S1.quote: I'm not precious about how things used to be done, because I don't know how they used to be done.
S1.fieldNote: He turns his newness into an advantage, which is a striking twist on being junior at 58. He is pragmatic about losers and winners without blaming anyone. His instinct to teach a colleague comes straight from his years showing customers the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, hold on, this is too quick for anyone, and we'd better have a plan for all the people out of work. I'd still say the technology's amazing, but I'd say the speed is the problem. I'd be talking about it all the time, Selin would be sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone by 60 and I'm fine with that, I've got money. What makes me uneasy is the chaos. Everybody losing work at once means nobody's buying cars, haircuts, nice chicken. Selin's salon would struggle, and our savings could take a hit if the markets go mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd move some savings out of shares and into cash, and the rest into a mix including the robot and AI companies, because if they're taking everything, I want a slice. I'd tell Selin to keep the salon lean, no new chair or new hire. Once it arrived, I'd try to get work as one of the people who run or check the robots on farms nearby, for as long as that lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me. Wary of everyone else going down at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short window take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time to retrain properly. With five or ten years, I could become a proper robot technician. With two, I'd be learning on the job while the job disappears. It'd be like trying to sell a model that's already being discontinued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy shares in the companies taking the jobs. Does that feel strange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe a little. I'd want one for myself, it's the business I know. But I'd feel bad being on the winning side while Dev's on the losing one.

S2.say: I'd say this is too quick for anyone and we need a plan for everyone out of work. The technology is amazing, but the speed is the problem.
S2.think: My job's gone by 60 and I'm fine with that because I have money. What makes me uneasy is everyone losing work at once, so nobody buys cars, haircuts or good chicken, and my wife's salon struggles.
S2.do: Moves some savings to cash and puts the rest partly into AI and robot companies, and tells his wife to keep her salon lean. Once AGI arrives, looks for work running or checking robots on nearby farms while that lasts.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for himself but wary of everyone else going down at once.
S2.quote: It'd be like trying to sell a model that's already being discontinued.
S2.fieldNote: He plays the role of a sensible investor even in the fastest picture, but sees that his household's second income depends on other people's spending. He admits mixed feelings about profiting while his colleague loses out. The short window kills the proper retraining he'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent run-up, so let's be ready. I'd say get learning now, and I'd say it with a smile, because I'd be enjoying it. And I'd say the government needs a proper plan for people who can't switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good fit. I'd be 63, and I'd have time to become the farm's robot man and earn well doing it for a few years. Then I'd retire when the robots don't need me anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd start the college course on autonomous machines and get the spraying certificate. Next year I'd ask Northfield to make me the person in charge of the drone and any self-driving kit, with a pay bump. I'd move our savings slowly into a mix, including the tech companies, and keep a good cash cushion for Selin's salon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and pretty pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Selin say about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin would say I'm getting carried away, she always does. She'd be right sometimes. But she'd also remember I said phones would sell cars before anyone at the dealership believed me, and I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is this a plan or a bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of it's a bet, sure. But it's a cheap one, a few evening classes and a bit of risk in the savings. If it goes wrong, I'm 63 with a paid-off house. That's not a bad place to lose a bet from.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a decent run-up, so let's be ready and get learning now. The government needs a proper plan for people who can't switch.
S3.think: For me it's a good fit: at 63, I'd have time to become the farm's robot man and earn well before retiring when the robots don't need me.
S3.do: Starts a college course on autonomous machines and gets his spraying certificate this winter, then asks the farm to put him in charge of drones and self-driving kit for more pay. Shifts savings gradually into a mix including tech firms, keeping cash for his wife's salon.
S3.quote: If it goes wrong, I'm 63 with a paid-off house. That's not a bad place to lose a bet from.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the ideal timeline for him, matching his planned exit with a chance to move up. He calls his plan a cheap bet, which shows how his money cushion lets him take risks. His wife is his reality check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the people who use it will do fine. I'd keep pushing people at work to learn. I'd say the government should start the retraining money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd retire at 65, a few years before it fully lands, and I'd have had a good run with the drones and the new kit. I'd be thinking about our kids' jobs more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year one, but slower: the course, the certificate, the drone job. I'd keep investing a bit each year in a broad fund, nothing fancy. And I'd plan to retire at 65 as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son, Emre, is an accountant, and I'd say his job's more at risk than mine ever was. I'd tell him to learn the tools now and get close to the clients, because people still buy from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your own thinking might be wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I might be wrong about how much people will still buy from people. That's my whole career talking. I'd admit I don't know.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and the people who use it will do fine. The government should start the retraining money now.
S4.think: It's comfortable for me: I'd retire at 65 before it fully lands, after a good run with the new kit. I'd think more about our children's jobs than mine.
S4.do: Follows the same plan as the five-year picture, more slowly: the course, the certificate and the drone role. Invests a little each year in a broad fund and plans to retire at 65 as normal.
S4.quote: Our son, Emre, is an accountant, and I'd say his job's more at risk than mine ever was.
S4.fieldNote: His worry flips to his son's office job, which he sees as more exposed than farm work. He is honest that his belief in 'people buy from people' comes from his sales career and may be wrong. The long window simply gives him a comfortable path to retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the chaos, everyone out at once, nobody spending. What would help is the government having a plan ready before it happens: money to keep people going, and real training places, not a waiting list. And I'd want a rule that small businesses like Selin's salon get help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked whether I'd go back to selling cars. No chance. I'd rather pick dead chickens out of a shed at six in the morning than hit another monthly target. That surprised me more than anything.

headlineQuote: I'd rather pick dead chickens out of a shed at six in the morning than hit another monthly target.
portrait: Aaron Yilmaz is 58 and sold cars for 28 years before starting as the most junior hand at Northfield Farms, a large grain and chicken operation. He uses AI every day to learn the job faster and treats new technology like a test drive, eager to try it. Financially comfortable, he plans to become the farm's drone and robot man and to invest some savings in technology firms. Only the two-year AGI picture makes him uneasy, because of the chaos of everyone losing work at once and the hit to his wife's salon. In the slower pictures he is calm and even optimistic, though he worries more about his son's accounting job than his own.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because of the chaos of everyone losing work at once and nobody spending.
whatWouldHelp: A government plan ready in advance, with money to keep people going, real training places and help for small businesses like his wife's salon.
